Seminar on Quillen’s proof of the Quillen-Suslin Theorem

Warren Dicks Address: Departament de Matemàtiques,
Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona,
E-08193 Bellaterra (Barcelona), SPAIN
Email address: dicks@mat.uab.cat
Home page:    http://mat.uab.cat/~dicks/

Let KK be a field, and nn be a positive integer. [Serre 1955, p. 243] remarked “On ignore s’il existe des K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]-modules projectifs de type fini qui ne soient pas libres.”. Motivated by this remark, [Quillen 1976] and [Suslin 1976] independently showed that every finitely generated, projective K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]-module is free, a result that is now known as the Quillen-Suslin theorem. [Lam 2006] gave an extensive collection of proofs and related results that were available 30 years later.

We construct an idempotent-matrix-based version of Quillen’s proof by translating most of Paul Roberts’ geometry-free proof of Horrocks’ theorem and translating part of Moshe Roitman’s proof of Quillen’s extension theorem. We described all of this in the Bedford College Ring Theory Study Group in the autumn term of 1977, and gave the participants copies of the three-page handout [Dicks 1977] later cited by [Lam 2006, pp.160,201\mkern 1.0mu160,\mkern 0.0mu201]. The present write-up includes minor changes and three pages of introductory material.

1 Definitions and Notation.

(i).(i). As Bourbaki intended, we let ℕ\mathbb{N} denote the set of finite cardinals; that is, ℕ:={0,1,2,,…}\mathbb{N}:=\{0,1,2,,\ldots\}.

(i​i).(ii). By a ring RR, we mean an associative ring with 11. A left RR-module MM is said to be RR-free (resp. RR-projective, resp. finitely RR-generated) if MM is a free (resp. projective, resp. finitely generated) left RR-module. For any subring R0R_{0} of RR, if M​≃𝑅​R⊗R0M0M\underset{R}{\simeq}R\otimes_{R_{0}}M_{0} for some left R0R_{0}-module M0M_{0}, then, for any ideal JJ of RR, we have (R/J)⊗RM≃R/J(R/J)⊗R0M0.(R/J)\otimes_{R}M\underset{R/J}{\simeq}(R/J)\otimes_{R_{0}}M_{0}. If, moreover, the natural map R0→R/JR_{0}\to R/J is bijective, then R0⊗RM​≃R0​M0R_{0}\otimes_{R}M\underset{R_{0}}{\simeq}M_{0}; here, M0M_{0} is uniquely determined by MM up to R0R_{0}-isomorphism, and, if MM is a finitely generated, projective left RR-module, then M0M_{0} is a finitely generated, projective left R0R_{0}-module.

(i​i​i).(iii). Whenever RR is a commutative ring, the following will apply: R⁡[x]R[x] denotes the polynomial ring over RR in one central variable denoted xx; R⁡(x)R(x) denotes the localization of R⁡[x]R[x] at the set of all monic polynomials in R⁡[x]R[x]; Max⁡(R)\operatorname{Max}(R) denotes the set of all maximal proper ideals of RR; and, for each 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R), R𝔪R_{\mathfrak{m}} denotes the localization of RR at R−𝔪R{-}\mathfrak{m}, the complement of 𝔪\mathfrak{m} in RR. Also, we shall say the following: RR is a domain if RR is nonzero and RR has no nonzero zerodivisors; RR is a Dedekind domain if RR is a domain and, for each 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R), the localization R𝔪R_{\mathfrak{m}} is a PID; and RR is local if RR has a unique maximal proper ideal. ∎

2 Review.

Let RR be a ring.

(i).(i). Let m,n∈ℕm,\,n\in{\mathbb{N}}. We write m​Rn\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n} to denote the set of all m×nm\times n matrices over RR. We give n​Rn\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n} the standard ring structure. We set Rn:=1​RnR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}:=\hbox{}^{1}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}, a free left RR-module. For each A∈m​RnA\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}, right multiplication by AA gives an RR-linear map Rm​→𝐴​RnR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}\overset{A\,\,}{\to}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}, whose image will be denoted Rm⋅AR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}A. Conversely, every RR-linear map Rm​→𝛼​RnR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}\overset{\alpha}{\to}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n} is given by right multiplication by a unique A∈m​RnA\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}; we shall view AA and α\alpha as interchangeable. ∎

(i​i).(ii). Let n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and E∈n​RnE\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n} such that E2=EE\mkern 1.0mu^{2}=E; we say that EE is idempotent. We now show that Rn⋅ER\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E is a finitely generated, projective left RR-module.

It suffices to show that Rn=Rn⋅E⊕Rn⋅(In−E)R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}=R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E\oplus R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}(I_{n}{-}E) as left RR-modules. It is clear that Rn=Rn⋅E+Rn⋅(In−E)R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}=R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E+R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}(I_{n}{-}E), since each A∈RnA\in R\mkern 2.0mu^{n} equals A⋅E+A⋅(In−E)A{\cdot}E+A{\cdot}(I_{n}{-}E). To see that Rn⋅E∩Rn⋅(In−E)={0}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E\cap R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}(I_{n}{-}E)=\{0\}, notice that this intersection is annihilated by right multiplication by In−EI_{n}{-}E and by right multiplication by EE; hence it is annihilated by right multiplication by E+(In−E)=InE+(I_{n}{-}E)=I_{n}. (i​i​i).(iii). Let PP be a finitely generated, projective left RR-module; thus, there exist an n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and a left RR-module QQ such that

Rn​≃𝑅​P⊕QR^{n}\underset{R}{\simeq}P{\oplus}Q. We now show that there exists an idempotent E∈n​RnE\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n} such that P​≃𝑅​Rn⋅EP\underset{R}{\simeq}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E.

Also, P=(Rn)​α​≃𝑅​((Rn)​α)​β=Rn⋅EP=(R\mkern 2.0mu^{n})\alpha\underset{R}{\simeq}((R\mkern 2.0mu^{n})\alpha)\beta=R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E.∎

(i​v).(iv). For idempotent matrices EE, FF over RR,

we write E​∼𝑅​FE\underset{R}{\sim}F to mean that there exist matrices AA, BB over RR such that A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E and B⋅A=FB{\cdot}A=F.

Let mm and nn be elements of ℕ{\mathbb{N}}, EE an idempotent element of m​Rm\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}, and FF an idempotent element of n​Rn\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}. We now show that E​∼𝑅​FE\underset{R}{\sim}F if and only if Rm⋅E​≃𝑅​Rn⋅FR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\underset{R}{\simeq}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F.

Consider first the situation where E​∼𝑅​FE\underset{R}{\sim}F. Here, there exist A∈m​RnA\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n} and B∈n​RmB\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{m} such that A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E and B⋅A=FB{\cdot}A=F. One fact that we shall use repeatedly throughout these notes is that E⋅A=A⋅FE{\cdot}A=A{\cdot}F here, since both sides equal A⋅B⋅AA{\cdot}B{\cdot}A. Now AA may be viewed as the RR-linear map Rm→RnR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}\to R\mkern 2.0mu^{n} given by right multiplication by AA. The RR-submodule Rm⋅ER\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E of RmR\mkern 2.0mu^{m} is carried by AA to (Rm⋅E)⋅A=(Rm⋅A)⋅F⊆Rn⋅F(R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E){\cdot}A=(R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}A){\cdot}F\subseteq R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F, giving an RR-linear map α:Rm⋅E→Rn⋅F\alpha{:\,}R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\to R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F. Similarly, BB gives an RR-linear map β:Rn⋅F→Rm⋅E\beta{:\,}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F\to R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E. The total effect of applying α\alpha and then β\beta to Rm⋅ER\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E is to right multiply by A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E, which fixes all elements of Rm⋅ER\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E. Similarly β⋅α\beta{\cdot}\alpha acts as the identity endomorphism of Rn⋅FR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F. Hence, Rm⋅E​≃𝑅​Rn⋅FR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\underset{R}{\simeq}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F.

Finally, suppose that we have an RR-linear isomorphism Rm⋅E​→𝛼​Rn⋅FR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\overset{\alpha\,}{\to}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F. The composite Rm→𝐸Rm⋅E→𝛼Rn⋅F⊆RnR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}\xrightarrow{E}R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\xrightarrow{\alpha}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F\subseteq R\mkern 2.0mu^{n} acts as right multiplication by a unique A∈m​RnA\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}. The composite Rn→𝐹Rn⋅F→α−1Rm⋅E⊆RmR\mkern 2.0mu^{n}\xrightarrow{F}R\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}F\xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}}R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\subseteq R\mkern 2.0mu^{m} acts as right multiplication by a unique B∈n​RmB\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}. The composite A⋅BA{\cdot}B equals the composite Rm→𝐸Rm⋅E⊆RmR\mkern 2.0mu^{m}\xrightarrow{E}R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}{\cdot}E\subseteq R\mkern 2.0mu^{m}, which is right multiplication by EE; hence, A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E. Similarly B⋅A=FB{\cdot}A=F. Thus, E​∼𝑅​FE\underset{R}{\sim}F. ∎

(v).(v). It is now clear that ∼𝑅\underset{R}{\sim} is an equivalence relation on the set of all idempotent (square) matrices over RR. Also, the set of equivalence classes is in bijective correspondence with the collection of all isomorphism classes of all finitely generated, projective left RR-modules. ∎  □\Box

3 Lemma.

Let RR be a local commutative ring. Let 𝔪\mathfrak{m} denote the maximal proper ideal of RR. Set R¯:=R/𝔪\overline{R}:=R/\mathfrak{m}, the residue field, and let R→R¯R\to\overline{R}, r↦r¯r\mapsto\overline{r}, denote the quotient map. We extend the overline notation to polynomials and matrices. We identify R⁡(x)/(𝔪⋅R⁡(x))R(x)/(\mathfrak{m}{\cdot}R(x)) with R¯​(x)\overline{R}(x), which is the field of fractions of R¯​[x]\overline{R}[x].

(i)(i). Each element of R⁡(x)R(x) equals fg\frac{f}{g} for some f,g∈R⁡[x]f,\,g\in R[x] with gg monic. The

polynomial division algorithm says that, for any f,g∈R⁡[x]f,\,g\in R[x] with gg monic, there exist unique q,r∈R⁡[x]q,\,r\in R[x] such that f=g⋅q+rf=g{\cdot}\,q+r and deg⁡r<deg⁡g\operatorname{deg}r<\operatorname{deg}g, where deg⁡0:=−∞\operatorname{deg}0:=-\infty; here, qq

is uniquely determined by fg\frac{f}{g}, and we call qq the polynomial part of fg\frac{f}{g}, denoted [fg][\frac{f}{g}]. The map R⁡(x)→R⁡[x]R(x)\to R[x], fg↦[fg]\frac{f}{g}\mapsto[\frac{f}{g}], is an RR-linear retraction. We denote the kernel by R​(x)∘:={fg∈R⁡(x):deg⁡f<deg⁡g}R(x)_{\circ}:=\{\frac{f}{g}\in R(x):\operatorname{deg}f<\operatorname{deg}g\}, and obtain an RR-module decomposition R⁡(x)=R⁡[x]⊕R​(x)∘R(x)=R[x]\oplus R(x)_{\circ}. ∎

(i​i)(ii). For r∈Rr\in R, if r¯≠0¯\overline{r}\neq\overline{0}, then r∉𝔪r\notin\mathfrak{m}, hence R​rR\mkern 2.0mur is not a proper ideal of RR, and hence rr is invertible in RR. ∎

(i​i​i)(iii). Let n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. We now show that, for each invertible A∈n​R¯​(x)nA\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0mu\overline{R}(x)\mkern 0.0mu^{n}, there exists an invertible B∈n​R​(x)nB\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR(x)\mkern 0.0mu^{n} such that B¯=A\overline{B}=A; we say that the invertible matrix over R¯​(x)\overline{R}(x) lifts back to some invertible matrix over R⁡(x)R(x).

By (i​i)(ii) above, each invertible element of the field R¯\overline{R} lifts back to some invertible element of RR. It then follows that each invertible element of the field R¯​(x)\overline{R}(x) lifts back to some invertible element of R⁡(x)R(x). It then follows that each invertible elementary matrix over R¯​(x)\overline{R}(x) lifts back to some invertible elementary matrix over R⁡(x)R(x). Over the field R¯​(x)\overline{R}(x), each invertible matrix is a product of invertible elementary matrices, and, hence, lifts back to some invertible matrix over R⁡(x)R(x). ∎

(i​v)(iv). Let WW be an RR-module, and W′W^{\prime} be an RR-submodule of WW such that, firstly, W/W′W/W^{\prime} is finitely RR-generated, and, second, 𝔪⋅W+W′=W\mathfrak{m}{\cdot}W{+}W^{\prime}=W. We shall now show that W′=WW^{\prime}=W. (This is the local commutative case of one form of Nakayama’s Lemma.)

Since W/W′W/W^{\prime} is finitely RR-generated, there exists a smallest n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} such that there exist w1,…,wn∈Ww_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\in W such that R⋅w1+⋯+R⋅wn+W′=WR{\cdot}w_{1}{+}\cdots{+}R{\cdot}w_{n}+W^{\prime}=W. We want to show that n=0n=0. Suppose that n⩾1n\geqslant 1; it suffices to obtain a contradiction. Set W′′:=R⋅w2+⋯+R⋅wn+W′W^{\prime\prime}:=R{\cdot}w_{2}{+}\cdots{+}R{\cdot}w_{n}{+}W^{\prime}. Then W=R⋅w1+W′′W=R{\cdot}w_{1}{+}W^{\prime\prime}. By the minimality of nn, W′′≠WW^{\prime\prime}\neq W; hence, w1∉W′′w_{1}\not\in W^{\prime\prime}. Now w1∈W=𝔪⋅W+W′=𝔪⋅(R⋅w1+W′′)+W′⊆𝔪⋅w1+W′′w_{1}\in W=\mathfrak{m}{\cdot}W{+}W^{\prime}=\mathfrak{m}{\cdot}(R{\cdot}w_{1}{+}W^{\prime\prime}){+}W^{\prime}\subseteq\mathfrak{m}{\cdot}w_{1}{+}W^{\prime\prime}. Hence, there exists some r∈𝔪r\in\mathfrak{m} such that w1∈r⋅w1+W′′w_{1}\in r{\cdot}w_{1}{+}W^{\prime\prime}, and than (1−r)⋅w1∈W′′(1{-}r){\cdot}w_{1}\in W^{\prime\prime}. By (i​i)(ii) above, 1−r1{-}r is invertible in RR, since 1−r¯=1¯−0¯≠0¯\overline{1{-}r}=\overline{1}{-}\overline{0}\neq\overline{0}. Hence, w1∈(1−r)−1⋅W′′⊆W′′w_{1}\in(1{-}r)^{-1}{\cdot}W^{\prime\prime}\subseteq W^{\prime\prime}, which contradicts w1∉W′′w_{1}\not\in W^{\prime\prime}. ∎

(v)(v). We now give an elementary proof that if the local commutative ring RR is a PID, then R⁡(x)R(x) is a PID. (This is the local case of [Quillen 1976, Lemma 2].)

If RR is a field, then R⁡(x)R(x) is the field of fractions of R⁡[x]R[x], which is clearly a PID; thus, we may assume that the local PID RR is not a field. Here 𝔪=R⋅p\mathfrak{m}=R{\cdot}p for some nonzero p∈Rp\in R. Then pp is irreducible in RR, and each nonzero element of RR has a unique expression as u⋅pnu{\cdot}p^{n} where n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and u∈R−R⋅pu\in R{-}R{\cdot}p. Each nonzero element of R⁡(x)R(x) has a unique expression as f⋅pnf{\cdot}p^{n} where n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and f∈R⁡(x)−R⁡(x)⋅pf\in R(x){-}R(x){\cdot}p. We identified R⁡(x)/(R⁡(x)⋅p)=R¯​(x)R(x)/(R(x){\cdot}p)=\overline{R}(x), the field of fractions of R¯​[x]\overline{R}[x]; thus, R⁡(x)⋅p∈Max⁡(R⁡(x))R(x){\cdot}p\in\operatorname{Max}(R(x)).

Let JJ be an arbitrary ideal of R⁡(x)R(x). We wish to show that JJ is a principal ideal of R⁡(x)R(x). We may assume that J≠{0}J\neq\{0\}. Let KK denote the field of fractions of RR. Then R⁡(x)R(x) lies in the field of fractions K⁡(x)K(x) of K⁡[x]K[x]. The subring R⁡(x)⋅KR(x){\cdot}K of K⁡(x)K(x) is a PID, since it is the localization of the PID K⁡[x]K[x] at the set of monic polynomials in R⁡[x]R[x]. As J⋅KJ{\cdot}K is a nonzero ideal of the PID R⁡(x)⋅KR(x){\cdot}K, there exists some nonzero f∈J⋅Kf\in J{\cdot}K such that J⋅K=R⁡(x)⋅K⋅fJ{\cdot}K=R(x){\cdot}K{\cdot}f. We may arrange that f∈J−J⋅pf\in J{-}J{\cdot}p. It suffices to show that J=R⁡(x)⋅fJ=R(x){\cdot}f. It is clear that R⁡(x)⋅K⋅f⊇J⊇R⁡(x)⋅fR(x){\cdot}K{\cdot}f\supseteq J\supseteq R(x){\cdot}f. Consider any nonzero element of JJ and express it as g⋅fg{\cdot}f for some g∈R⁡(x)⋅Kg\in R(x){\cdot}K; it suffices to show that g∈R⁡(x)g\in R(x). We may write g=p−n⋅g′g=p^{-n}{\cdot}g^{\prime}, where n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}} and g′∈R⁡(x)−R⁡(x)⋅pg^{\prime}\in R(x){-}R(x){\cdot}p; it suffices to show that −n⩾0-n\geqslant 0. Thus, pp and (hence) pnp^{n} become invertible in R⁡(x)/(R⁡(x)⋅g′)R(x)/(R(x){\cdot}g^{\prime}). As g′⋅f=pn⋅g⋅f∈pn⋅Jg^{\prime}{\cdot}f=p^{n}{\cdot}g{\cdot}f\in p^{n}{\cdot}J, we see that g′g^{\prime}, pnp^{n}, and (hence) 11 all lie in the ideal {h∈R⁡(x):h⋅f∈pn⋅J}\{h\in R(x):h{\cdot}f\in p^{n}{\cdot}J\} of R⁡(x)R(x). Now 1⋅f∈pn⋅J1{\cdot}f\in p^{n}{\cdot}J, and this contradicts f∉J⋅pf\not\in J{\cdot}p. ∎  □\Box

By [Quillen 1976, Theorem 3], if RR is a commutative ring and PP is a finitely generated, projective R⁡[x]R[x]-module such that R⁡(x)⊗R⁡[x]PR(x){\otimes}_{R[x]}P is R⁡(x)R(x)-free, then PP is R⁡[x]R[x]-free. Using [Horrocks 1964, Theorem 1], M. Pavaman Murthy [Bass 1973, Lemma on p. 24] had proved the case where RR is noetherian and local, which is already sufficient for our main purpose. Here, we shall prove the case where RR is local.

4 Theorem.

If RR is a local commutative ring and PP is a finitely generated, projective R⁡[x]R[x]-module such that R⁡(x)⊗R⁡[x]PR(x){\otimes}_{R[x]}P is R⁡(x)R(x)-free, then PP is R⁡[x]R[x]-free.

Proof ((Paul Roberts)).

We use the notation of Lemma 3 above.

By Review 2(i​i​i)(iii) above, there exist an n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and an idempotent E∈n​R​[x]nE\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR[x]\mkern 0.0mu^{n} such that P​≃R⁡[x]​R​[x]n⋅EP\underset{R[x]}{\simeq}R[x]\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E; hence, R⁡(x)⊗R⁡[x]P​≃R⁡(x)​R​(x)n⋅ER(x)\otimes_{R[x]}\mkern-3.0muP\underset{R(x)}{\simeq}R(x)\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E. By Review 2(i​v)(iv) above, since R⁡(x)⊗R⁡[x]PR(x)\otimes_{R[x]}P is R⁡(x)R(x)-free, there exist an m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}, an A∈n​R​(x)mA\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR(x)\mkern 0.0mu^{m}, and a B∈m​R​(x)nB\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR(x)\mkern 0.0mu^{n} such that A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E and B⋅A=ImB{\cdot}A=I_{m}. Also by Review 2(i​v)(iv) above, to show that PP is R⁡[x]R[x]-free it suffices to show that there exist an A′′∈n​R​[x]mA^{\prime\prime}\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR[x]\mkern 0.0mu^{m} and a B′′∈m​R​[x]nB^{\prime\prime}\in\hbox{}^{m}\mkern-3.0muR[x]\mkern 2.0mu^{n} such that A′′⋅B′′=EA^{\prime\prime}{\cdot}B^{\prime\prime}=E and B′′⋅A′′=ImB^{\prime\prime}{\cdot}A^{\prime\prime}=I_{m}.

Here, E¯∈n​R¯​[x]n\overline{E}\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-2.0mu\overline{R}[x]\mkern 0.0mu^{n}. Now R¯​[x]\overline{R}[x] is a PID; hence, finitely generated, projective R¯​[x]\overline{R}[x]-modules are R¯​[x]\overline{R}[x]-free. By Quillen’s extension theorem [Quillen 1976, Theorem 1], [Roitman 1979, Theorem], if RR is a commutative ring and PP is a finitely presented R⁡[x]R[x]-module such that, for each 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R), R𝔪​[x]⊗R⁡[x]PR_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]{\otimes}_{R[x]}P is R𝔪​[x]R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]-free (or, more generally, R𝔪​[x]R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]-isomorphic to R𝔪​[x]⊗R𝔪P𝔪R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]{\otimes\hskip-1.0pt}_{R_{\mathfrak{m}}}\hskip-2.0ptP_{\mathfrak{m}} for some R𝔪R_{\mathfrak{m}}-module P𝔪P_{\mathfrak{m}}), then PP is R⁡[x]R[x]-isomorphic to R⁡[x]⊗RP′R[x]{\otimes_{R}}P\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime} for some RR-module P′P\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime}. Here, all that we shall prove is the domain case of the result obtained by combining Quillen’s extension theorem with Theorem 4 above.

5 Theorem.

If RR is a domain and PP is a finitely generated, projective R⁡[x]R[x]-module such that R𝔪​(x)⊗R⁡[x]PR_{\mathfrak{m}}(x){\otimes}_{R[x]}P\, is R𝔪​(x)R_{\mathfrak{m}}(x)-free for

each 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R), then P​≃R⁡[x]​R​[x]⊗RP′P\underset{R[x]}{\simeq}R[x]\otimes_{R}\mkern-3.0muP\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime} for some finitely generated, projective RR-module P′P\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime}.

Set R⁡[x,y]:=R⁡[x]​[y]=R⁡[y]​[x]R[x,y]:=R[x][y]=R[y][x]. For each f∈R⁡[x,y]f\in R[x,y], we write (y↦f):R⁡[x,y]→R⁡[x,y](y\mapsto f){:\,}R[x,y]\to R[x,y], g↦g(y↦f)g\mapsto g^{(y\mapsto f)}, to denote the unique ring endomorphism of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] which sends yy to ff and fixes each element of R⁡[x]R[x]. We define (x↦f)(x\mapsto f) analogously. We extend these maps to matrices coordinate-wise.

By Review 2(i​i​i)(iii) above, there exist an n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and an idempotent E∈n​R​[x]nE\in\hbox{}^{n}\mkern-3.0muR[x]\mkern 0.0mu^{n} such that P​≃R⁡[x]​R​[x]n⋅EP\underset{R[x]}{\simeq}R[x]\mkern 2.0mu^{n}{\cdot}E. Here, E(x↦x+j⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+j{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E, and applying (x↦x+j′⋅y)(x\mapsto x+j^{\prime}{\cdot}y) yields E(x↦x+j′⋅y+j⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​E(x↦x+j′⋅y)E^{(x\mapsto x+j^{\prime}{\cdot}y+j{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E^{(x\mapsto x+j^{\prime}{\cdot}y)}. Since E(x↦x+j′⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+j^{\prime}{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E, we see that E(x↦x+j′⋅y+j⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+j^{\prime}{\cdot}y+j{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E, whence j+j′∈Jj+j^{\prime}\in J. Now consider any j∈Jj\in J and r∈Rr\in R. Since EE is a matrix over R⁡[x]R[x], applying (y↦r⋅y)(y\mapsto r{\cdot}\,y) to E(x↦x+j⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+j{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E yields E(x↦x+j⋅r⋅y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+j{\cdot}r{\cdot}y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E, whence j⋅r∈Jj{\cdot}r\in J. Hence, JJ is an ideal of RR.

Consider an arbitrary 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R). By hypothesis, R𝔪​(x)⊗R𝔪​[x](R𝔪​[x]⊗R⁡[x]P)R_{\mathfrak{m}}(x)\otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]}(R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x]{\otimes}_{R[x]}P) is R𝔪​(x)R_{\mathfrak{m}}(x)-free. By Review 2(i​v)(iv) above, there exist matrices II, AA, and BB over R𝔪​[x]R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x] such that II is an identity matrix, A⋅B=EA{\cdot}B=E, and B⋅A=IB{\cdot}A=I. We extend our ring-endomorphism notation from R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] to R𝔪​[x,y]R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x,y], and set C:=A⋅B(x↦x+y)C:=A{\cdot}B^{(x\mapsto x{+}y)} and D:=A(x↦x+y)⋅BD:=A^{(x\mapsto x{+}y)}{\cdot}B. Hence, C(y↦r⋅y)C^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)} is a matrix over R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]. Similarly, D(y↦r⋅y)D^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)} is a matrix over R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]. Over R𝔪​[x,y]R_{\mathfrak{m}}[x,y],

C(y↦r⋅y)⋅D(y↦r⋅y)\displaystyle C^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}D^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)} =A⋅B(x↦x+r⋅y)⋅A(x↦x+r⋅y)⋅B=A⋅(B⋅A)(x↦x+r⋅y)⋅B=A⋅I⋅B=E,\displaystyle=A{\cdot}B^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}A^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}B=A{\cdot}(B{\cdot}A)^{(x\mapsto x+r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}B=A{\cdot}I{\cdot}B=E,
D(y↦r⋅y)⋅C(y↦r⋅y)\displaystyle D^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}C^{(y\mapsto r{\cdot}y)} =A(x↦x+r⋅y)⋅B⋅A⋅B(x↦x+r⋅y)=A(x↦x+r⋅y)⋅I⋅B(x↦x+r⋅y)=E(x↦x+r⋅y).\displaystyle=A^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}B{\cdot}A{\cdot}B^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}=A^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}{\cdot}I{\cdot}B^{(x\mapsto x{+}r{\cdot}y)}=E^{(x\mapsto x+r{\cdot}y)}.

Hence, E​∼R⁡[x,y]​E(x↦x+r⋅y)E\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E^{(x\mapsto x+r{\cdot}y)}; that is,

r∈Jr\in J. Since r∉𝔪r\not\in\mathfrak{m}, we have J⊈𝔪J\nsubseteq\mathfrak{m}. Since 𝔪∈Max⁡(R)\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(R) is arbitrary, 1∈J1\in J; that is, E(x↦x+y)​∼R⁡[x,y]​EE^{(x\mapsto x+y)}\underset{R[x,y]}{\sim}E. Thus,

there exist matrices A0A_{0}, B0B_{0} over R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] such that A0⋅B0=E(x↦x+y)A_{0}{\cdot}B_{0}=E^{(x\mapsto x+y)} and B0⋅A0=EB_{0}{\cdot}A_{0}=E. We now prove the result of [Quillen 1976, Theorem 4′4^{\prime}] and [Suslin 1976, Theorem 3].

6 The Quillen-Suslin Theorem.

Let n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, let KK be a Dedekind domain, let RR denote K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], and let PP be a finitely generated, projective RR-module. Then P​≃𝑅​R⊗KP0P\underset{R}{\simeq}R\otimes_{K}\mkern-3.0muP_{0} for some finitely generated, projective KK-module P0P_{0}. If KK is a PID, then P0P_{0} is KK-free and PP is RR-free.

Proof ((Quillen)). We argue by induction on nn. As the result is clear for n=0n=0, we may assume that n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and that the result holds with n−1n{-}1 in place of nn.

Set X:={x2,…,xn}X:=\{x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\}. Consider an arbitrary 𝔪∈Max⁡(K⁡[X])\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(K[X]). There then exists some 𝔪′∈Max⁡(K)\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Max}(K) such that 𝔪∩K⊆𝔪′\mathfrak{m}\cap K\subseteq\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}. By hypothesis, PP is a finitely generated, projective K​[x1]​[X]K[x_{1}][X]-module. We view K⁡[x1]​[X]⊆K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]K[x_{1}][X]\subseteq K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]. Then K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]⊗K​[x1]​[X]PK_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]\otimes_{K[x_{1}][X]}P is a finitely generated, projective K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]-module; it is K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]-free by the induction hypothesis, since K𝔪′​(x1)K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1}) is a PID by Lemma 3(v)(v) above, since K𝔪′K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}} is a local PID. We now view K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]⊆K​[X]𝔪​(x1)K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]\subseteq K[X]_{\mathfrak{m}}(x_{1}). Then K​[X]𝔪​(x1)⊗K𝔪′​(x1)​[X](K𝔪′​(x1)​[X]⊗K​[x1]​[X]P)K[X]_{\mathfrak{m}}(x_{1})\otimes_{K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]}\hskip-1.8pt(K_{\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}}(x_{1})[X]\otimes_{K[x_{1}][X]}P) is K​[X]𝔪​(x1)K[X]_{\mathfrak{m}}(x_{1})-free; that is, K​[X]𝔪​(x1)⊗K​[X]​[x1]PK[X]_{\mathfrak{m}}(x_{1})\otimes_{K[X][x_{1}]}\hskip-1.8ptP is K​[X]𝔪​(x1)K[X]_{\mathfrak{m}}(x_{1})-free. Since 𝔪∈Max⁡(K⁡[X])\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Max}(K[X]) is arbitrary, Theorem 5 above now shows that P​≃K​[X]​[x1]​K​[X]​[x1]⊗K⁡[X]P′P\mkern-5.0mu\underset{K[X][x_{1}]}{\simeq}K[X][x_{1}]\otimes_{K[X]}\mkern-3.0muP\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime} for some finitely generated, projective K⁡[X]K[X]-module P′P\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime}. By the induction hypothesis again, P′​≃K⁡[X]​K​[X]⊗KP0P\mkern 1.0mu^{\prime}\mkern-5.0mu\underset{K[X]}{\simeq}K[X]\otimes_{K}P_{0} for some finitely generated, projective KK-module P0P_{0}, and then P​≃K​[X]​[x1]​K​[X]​[x1]⊗KP0P\mkern-5.0mu\underset{K[X][x_{1}]}{\simeq}K[X][x_{1}]\otimes_{K}\mkern-3.0muP_{0}. ∎
